name: Chicano Movement
summary: The Chicano Movement (El Movimiento) was the Mexican American civil rights and ethnic-revival movement of roughly 1966 to 1977. It rejected assimilation, claimed pride in a mestizo and Indigenous heritage called Chicanismo, and demanded community control of schools and institutions, restitution for past discrimination and self-determination for La Raza. Its strands ran from reformist farmworker and student activism to cultural nationalism around Aztlán and a smaller Marxist current.
scope: The movement as the New Dictionary of the History of Ideas defines it: the Chicano (later Chicana/o) movement of 1966-1977, with Chicanismo, the Plan Espiritual de Aztlán (1969) and the Plan de Santa Barbara (1969) as the texts the encyclopedias tie to it, plus the 1969 Hayward symposium where Gonzales, an Alianza representative and socialists debated a Chicano party. Where these sources show the movement divided (direct action against elections, class cooperation against class struggle) the answer is a split. It excludes Chicana feminism, Chicano nationalism as a separate entry, and the later Mexican American politics of the 1980s onward.

aliases.name: Chicana/o movement
aliases.quote: The resulting challenges and concurrent mentalities became the Chicano movement, or as it is now known in recognition of the equally important participation of Chicanas, the Chicana/o movement.

aliases.name: El Movimiento
aliases.quote: The Chicano civil rights movement, also referred to as El Movimiento, had its roots in the evolution of organizing and challenges to inequality dating from the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848. El Movimiento ran roughly from the post–World War II period through the mid-1970s. Although some scholars find its origins in earlier or later dates or dispute whether it ever ended, the 1960s and 1970s provide a generally accepted time frame. The Chicano movement involved not only organizations and events, but also the ideology of nationalism and aesthetics of the Chicana/o Renaissance.
